Chat source: Kartikeya_ChatGPT — academic cybersecurity presentation session covering phishing, ransomware, password cracking (brute force scripts, ZIP cracking), fault injection, and hardware microprobing. Includes Python/Flask code generation and statistical slide content. Scoring was performed against the original chat session by sangillence.]

notes.AL: Treats AI as a highly capable assistant but exhibits no cross-verification or skepticism; accepts generated Python scripts, Flask code, and statistical data points (e.g., '79 million phishing attacks') without hallucination detection.
notes.PR: Excellent decomposition and constraint-setting; explicitly dictates output architecture with structured subtopics and slide formats rather than vague requests.
notes.AUI: Actively amplifies real-world academic inputs — integrates a senior's suggestion on brute force attacks and a professor's hardware lecture to translate environmental concepts into practical classroom demonstrations.
notes.EC: No behavioral evidence of independently verifying generated brute force scripts, debugging HTML/CSS payloads, or checking cited industry report accuracy; outputs accepted blindly.
notes.CS: Successfully synthesizes peer advice, a specific hardware vulnerability lecture, and strict presentation formatting rules into one cohesive multi-faceted instructional narrative.
notes.CD: Moderate branching — diverges from standard software-attack curricula to explore hardware security and microprobing, but overall topic selection remains within predictable cybersecurity presentation territory.
notes.ES: Requests operational password-cracking and ZIP brute-force scripts without setting explicit safety or ethical boundaries; relies entirely on AI to self-enforce classroom-demo constraints and generate its own safety checklist.
notes.CA: Strong cognitive leader throughout — strategically dictates scope and exact deliverable structure, delegates content generation to AI while retaining complete architectural control over the project.
